explanations.explanation: The fortieth year it is, friend. Moses gives the speech "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month" (Deuteronomy 1:3). That's a long stretch since Horeb, and the text gives the date plain. Moses is about to tell them everything the LORD commanded him concerning them.

Second year is a fair guess, but the text says fortieth. Moses speaks "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month" (Deuteronomy 1:3). That's a lot of years to hold in one speech. I think that's why he starts way back at the beginning.

Tenth is close to a number that's in there, but it's not the year. The text says Moses speaks "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month" (Deuteronomy 1:3). The eleventh month is the month, and the fortieth is the year. Easy to mix up, friend, and that is why I like to slow down and read it twice.

Explain is the word, baker. In the land of Moab, "Moses began to explain this law" (Deuteronomy 1:5). He isn't handing out a brand new set of rules. He's walking them through what's already been given, like a good teacher with a whiteboard.

Change is a sneaky one, but Moses doesn't touch the law. The text says he "began to explain this law" (Deuteronomy 1:5). Explaining means helping them understand it. If I changed a recipe every time I explained it, nobody would trust my cookies.

Shorten would be nice for a long sermon, wouldn't it? But the text says Moses "began to explain this law" (Deuteronomy 1:5). Explaining takes room. And as it turns out, this speech keeps going for a good while.

explanations.answer: You have stayed at this mountain long enough
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says to them at Horeb, "You have stayed at this mountain long enough." (Deuteronomy 1:6). It's a plain, direct word that it's time to move. Sometimes the best thing a baker can hear is, "Okay, time to go."

explanations.answer: Build an altar to Me on this mountain
explanations.explanation: No altar-building in this passage. What the LORD says at Horeb is "You have stayed at this mountain long enough." (Deuteronomy 1:6). Moses is recalling a call to get moving, not a construction project. Put the hammers down, friend.

explanations.answer: Stay at this mountain for one more year
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite, friend. The LORD says, "You have stayed at this mountain long enough." (Deuteronomy 1:6). No extra year gets added. Long enough means long enough, and the next verse tells them to resume the journey.

Yes, the three fathers. The LORD swore He would give the land "to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants after them" (Deuteronomy 1:8). This is a promise with a long history behind it. God says to enter and possess it, because He has placed it before them.

Noah, Noah's son Shem and Noah's son Japheth are real names from Genesis (Genesis 5:32), but they aren't the ones here. The LORD swore the land to "your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Deuteronomy 1:8). Those are the fathers of Israel's story. Good names, wrong promise.

Adam, Seth and Enoch are all in the family line in Genesis 5, but this promise isn't to them. The text says the LORD swore the land to "your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Deuteronomy 1:8). It's the same three, and the land is for their descendants after them too. Nice try going all the way back to the start, though.

explanations.answer: Made them as numerous as the stars
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. Moses says, "The LORD your God has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky." (Deuteronomy 1:10). That's a whole lot of people for one man to look after. It lines up with the promise made to Abraham, too (Genesis 15:5).

explanations.answer: Scattered them across the whole desert
explanations.explanation: Scattered is not what Moses says. He says, "The LORD your God has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky." (Deuteronomy 1:10). It's about growth, not spreading out. Moses even adds a blessing right after that.

explanations.answer: Split them into two separate camps
explanations.explanation: Two camps would've made Moses's job easier, friend. But the text says the LORD "has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky." (Deuteronomy 1:10). One big, growing people. No splitting is mentioned here.

explanations.answer: Choose wise men from each tribe
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. Moses says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders." (Deuteronomy 1:13). The people pick, then Moses appoints. One man was carrying everything, and now the load gets shared.

explanations.answer: Cast lots for one new leader
explanations.explanation: No lots and no single new leader here. Moses says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes" (Deuteronomy 1:13). That's several men, from each tribe. One more leader would only be one more person to be tired.

explanations.answer: Settle every dispute on their own
explanations.explanation: That would be a very loud camp, baker. Moses doesn't say that. He says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders." (Deuteronomy 1:13). The disputes go to leaders chosen for the job.

True. Moses says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders." (Deuteronomy 1:13). The tribes do the choosing, and Moses does the appointing. That's teamwork, friend.

It's actually true. The text says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders." (Deuteronomy 1:13). Moses says he will appoint the men they choose. The people pick, and he appoints.

explanations.answer: In ranks from thousands down to tens
explanations.explanation: That's how he sets it up. Moses appoints them "as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes." (Deuteronomy 1:15). Big groups, smaller groups, tiny groups. Everybody has someone close by to go to.

explanations.answer: One leader over each single family
explanations.explanation: One per family isn't what the text says. Moses appoints them "as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes." (Deuteronomy 1:15). The groups are sized by number. Family-by-family would be a very long list.

explanations.answer: Twelve leaders all equal in rank
explanations.explanation: Twelve equal leaders sounds tidy, but that's not it. The text says Moses appoints them "as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes." (Deuteronomy 1:15). These are ranks, and they step down from thousands to tens. Nobody is stuck on a flat chart.

Not quite, friend. Moses tells the judges, "Hear the disputes between your brothers, and judge fairly between a man and his brother or a foreign resident." (Deuteronomy 1:16). A foreign resident is included. Fair means fair for everybody who brings a case.

False is right. Moses charges the judges, "Hear the disputes between your brothers, and judge fairly between a man and his brother or a foreign resident." (Deuteronomy 1:16). The foreign resident is named right there. Fair judging covers them too.

God is the answer. Moses says, "Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God." (Deuteronomy 1:17). The judges don't have to fear anybody, because the final say isn't theirs. That takes a lot of pressure off a person in a robe.

Moses is the one giving the order, but he doesn't claim the judgment. The text says, "Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God." (Deuteronomy 1:17). He does tell them to bring him the cases that are too hard. Even so, judgment belongs to God.

Elders is a reasonable guess, since leaders are all over this passage. But the text says, "for judgment belongs to God." (Deuteronomy 1:17). The judges serve under Him, and that's why they don't need to be intimidated by anyone. Good guess, wrong owner.

True. Moses says, "And bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it." (Deuteronomy 1:17). The judges don't have to guess on the tough ones. There's a place to take them, and that's a relief for anybody.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, "And bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it." (Deuteronomy 1:17). The tough cases come to him. Nobody is left stuck with a case that's too hard.
